title: Explicit-state model checking (SPIN)
description: SPIN exhaustively explores every reachable state of a concurrent protocol model written in Promela, checking for deadlocks, assertion violations, and LTL properties. If a bug exists in the model, SPIN finds the shortest path to it — protocols are debugged before they're built.
method: Model the protocol in Promela; specify properties in LTL; SPIN explores the state graph (with partial-order reduction); violations come with trails.
usage: Model protocols before implementing; keep models abstract enough to check; replay trails as tests.

demo.code:
print('SPIN: 1,204,882 states explored, 0 errors')
print('property G(request -> F grant): HOLDS')

title: Alloy relational modeling
description: Alloy models systems as relations and checks assertions within a bounded scope, generating instances or counterexamples automatically. Its analyzer turns 'is my design consistent?' into a SAT problem — lightweight formal methods that fit in a design review.
method: Write signatures and facts; assert properties; the analyzer translates to SAT within a scope; counterexamples are concrete instances.
usage: Model data-structure and access-control designs; check within small scopes; inspect counterexamples as design feedback.

demo.code:
print('Alloy: check NoOrphanedFiles for scope 5')
print('counterexample found: file with no owner -> fix model')

title: State-space hashing and compression
description: Explicit-state checkers store billions of visited states; bitstate hashing and collapse compression shrink each state to bits, trading a tiny probability of hash collision for 10-100x memory savings. SPIN's bitstate mode checks enormous spaces on ordinary machines.
method: Hash states into a bit array (bitstate) or compress common prefixes (collapse); accept the quantified collision risk; verify critical results with exact mode.
usage: Use approximate modes for bug hunting, exact mode for final certification of critical properties.

demo.code:
print('bitstate: 2^27 bits covers 4.1B-state space in 16MB')
print('collision risk < 1e-6 -> acceptable for bug hunting')

title: LTL property specification patterns
description: Writing temporal properties from scratch is error-prone; specification patterns (Dwyer et al.) provide proven templates — 'absence', 'response', 'precedence' — with known-correct LTL/CTL formalizations. Engineers pick the pattern matching their intent instead of hand-rolling temporal logic.
method: Map the requirement to a pattern; instantiate with your propositions; use the pattern's vetted formalization directly.
usage: Keep a pattern catalog for the team; review any hand-rolled temporal formula twice.

demo.code:
print('requirement: every request gets a grant')
print('pattern: Response -> LTL: G(request -> F grant)')

title: Assume-guarantee compositional checking
description: Checking a whole system at once doesn't scale; assume-guarantee splits it: prove each component correct assuming its environment meets an interface contract, then check the contracts compose. Components are checked once, in isolation, and the composition proof is small.
method: Specify assume/guarantee contracts per component; model-check each against its contract; verify contract compatibility at composition.
usage: Invest in good interface contracts; they're the reusable asset across component versions.

demo.code:
print('component A: proved under assume(env fair)')
print('component B: guarantees fairness -> contracts compose: SYSTEM HOLDS')

title: Model checking in CI pipelines
description: Model checking earns its keep when it runs on every change: specs live next to code, the checker runs in CI with bounded scopes, and regressions in the design fail the build like test failures. Amazon's TLA+ CI integration is the template — formal specs as living CI artifacts.
method: Check in specs + models; CI runs the checker with fixed bounds/seeds; failures block merge; bound increases are deliberate decisions.
usage: Keep check times CI-friendly (bound the model); treat spec failures as design bugs, not noise.

demo.code:
print('CI: TLC check, bound 4, seed 42 -> 88,231 states, 0 violations (41s)')
print('spec regression: none -> MERGE')

title: Counterexample-guided abstraction refinement (CEGAR)
description: CEGAR starts with a coarse abstraction of the system; if the abstract check finds a violation, it tests whether the counterexample is real — spurious ones refine the abstraction, real ones are reported. The abstraction grows only as precise as needed, automatically.
method: Abstract -> model check -> validate counterexample -> refine on spurious -> repeat; SLAM/SDV applied this to Windows drivers.
usage: Use for software with huge concrete state spaces; let refinement be driven by spurious counterexamples.

demo.code:
print('CEGAR iteration 3: spurious cex -> predicate added')
print('iteration 4: abstract check PASSES -> property holds')

title: Partial-order reduction
description: Concurrent systems explode combinatorially because independent actions interleave. Partial-order reduction observes that independent actions commute, so the checker explores one representative interleaving per equivalence class — often shrinking the state space by orders of magnitude without losing bugs.
method: Compute action independence; explore ample/persistent sets; preserve at least one interleaving per Mazurkiewicz trace.
usage: Enable POR in the checker; define independence accurately (wrong independence = missed bugs).

demo.code:
print('without POR: 48M states; with POR: 1.2M states')
print('same bugs found — 40x reduction')
